source.title: Crosscoding Through Time: Tracking Emergence & Consolidation Of Linguistic Representations Throughout LLM Pretraining
source.authors: Deniz Bayazit; Aaron Mueller; Antoine Bosselut

page_placements.theme: Feature abstraction grows with depth and over pretraining

record.tranche_reason: The study tracks feature changes across pretraining checkpoints, not SAE dictionary-size changes. It does not test whether features split as dictionary size increases, whether child features partition parent inputs, or whether the SAE objective causes splitting.
record.gate_note: The crosscoder comparisons and annotations report feature emergence, persistence, and changing levels of abstraction across training checkpoints. These results concern a related but different question from splitting across dictionary sizes. Benchmark performance and reconstruction statistics are not results on the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains crosscoders at one fixed dictionary size (16,384) across pretraining checkpoints of Pythia-1B, OLMo-1B and BLOOM-1B. It tracks feature emergence, persistence and abstraction over training, not splitting with dictionary size, absorption, or the effect of SAE objectives. It mentions splitting nowhere, so none of its results bear on V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that crosscoders plus RelIE can trace when features emerge, persist and disappear during pretraining. Monolingual models move from token-specific detectors to high-level syntactic features, and multilingual models consolidate features into crosslingual ones.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse crosscoders with a joint feature space across model checkpoints, plus Relative Indirect Effects; it does not perform an SAE dictionary-size sweep or test splitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Checkpoint selection can influence the takeaways; the analysis focuses on middle-layer activations and benchmark-defined tasks. The authors also note that early checkpoints can be harder to interpret.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-1B, top task-relevant crosscoder features shift from token-specific and morphological detectors toward abstract grammatical detectors across checkpoints, even after accuracy plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-relevant features become more abstract over pretraining, and they keep changing after benchmark performance plateaus.

fits_no_version.finding: In OLMo-1B, features move toward more abstract noun-phrase detectors, while surface-level detectors such as newline detectors persist.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abstraction increases over pretraining, but some surface-level features persist.

fits_no_version.finding: In BLOOM-1B, crosslingual top-10 feature overlap increases by 341B for Latin-script languages; Hindi and Arabic stay more language-specific.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-specific features consolidate into crosslingual features over pretraining, with less sharing for morphologically complex or low-resource languages.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study states that checkpoint selection affects takeaways, early checkpoints can be harder to interpret, annotations involve subjectivity, and integrated-gradient attribution does not strictly guarantee causality. Findings are limited to selected benchmarks and the studied middle layers.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were omitted. Reconstruction statistics, benchmark performance, and feature-importance validation were not included because they do not test dictionary-size splitting.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep. Only one crosscoder size (2^14) is used.
No size-related splitting is measured in any model or open SAE release.
Nested families from size-driven splitting, and their geometry, are not examined.
No parent/child firing or absorption analysis, and no size or sparsity variation.
No comparison of latents across dictionary sizes.
Only an L1 crosscoder is used. There is no objective comparison such as Matryoshka SAEs.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for the claim. Its crosscoders use an L1 objective at a fixed dictionary size of 16,384, so it says nothing about dictionary-size splitting. The record's relation 'discusses' is generous, since the paper never discusses feature splitting; 'cites_only' (it cites Bricken et al.) would also be defensible. Tranche T6 is correct.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary SAE dictionary size or test whether larger-dictionary features split a smaller feature's inputs or lie near its direction.
Although it uses several model families, it does not test size-related splitting in large models or open SAE releases.
The study does not test whether size-related split features form nested, geometrically close families mirroring a conceptual hierarchy.
The study does not test parent-child firing overlap or whether changing SAE size or sparsity resolves absorption.
The study does not compare latent decompositions across SAE dictionary sizes or test whether larger SAEs add novel latents.
The study does not test whether splitting is an artifact of the SAE objective or compare objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: Pythia-1B
rows.operation_detail: Annotated task-relevant crosscoder features across checkpoints
rows.measure: Qualitative change in annotated feature types across checkpoints
rows.value: The annotations describe early token-specific and morphological detectors, followed by more abstract grammatical and semantic detectors at later checkpoints; some task-relevant features continue to emerge after performance plateaus.
rows.note: This is feature evolution across training checkpoints, not splitting across dictionary sizes.
rows.check: This is feature evolution across training checkpoints at a fixed dictionary size. It cannot show size-driven splitting, so 'observed' only describes the paper's own finding, not any claim version.

rows.value: Early features are often language-specific; later checkpoints include more crosslingual features, while Hindi and Arabic retain more language-specific representations for the studied layer and task.
rows.note: This measures feature evolution across training and languages, not dictionary-size splitting.

relation.reason: The text never discusses feature splitting, absorption or dictionary-size effects. Its only 'split' is 'validation split'. It cites Bricken et al. 2023 (Towards Monosemanticity) only as background for SAEs.

tranche.reason: Crosscoders at one fixed dictionary size (2^14 = 16,384) are tracked over pretraining checkpoints. There is no dictionary-size sweep and no test of splitting, absorption or SAE objectives.

source_check.notes: This is a checkpoint-evolution study using crosscoders at a fixed dictionary size (16,384) on Pythia-1B, OLMo-1B and BLOOM-1B. Its token-specific-to-abstract shifts happen over training time, not across dictionary size, so they do not bear on any splitting version. The final OLMo checkpoint is 3T in the text and 3048B in the tables.

statements.problem: None. The Pythia part matches the Table 1 caption ('even after accuracy plateaus'), the Table 10 caption and §7.1. The OLMo part matches the Fig. 6 caption ('newline detectors, persist across training') and Table 11, which hedges with 'may be retaining'.
